newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin nature lovers try to stop Love Parade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin nature lovers try to stop Love Parade.

text.p: Bird lovers have taken on the Love Parade.
Berlin's greatest tourist attraction since the Berlin Wall may be cancelled this year because environmentalists have launched a legal challenge to prevent it from taking place in a nature reserve.

More than one million music lovers from around the world are expected to crowd into Berlin on July 12 for the eighth annual Love Parade, a six km (four mile)-long gyrating party of dancing, drinking and outlawed substances.

Fearing that "ravers" will trample plants and pollute the historic Tiergarten park next to the route with human waste, the BUND environmental group has petitioned a court for an injunction to stop it taking place there.

"Last year's parade caused extensive and permanent damage to the fragile ecosystem of the Tiergarten," said BUND spokeswoman Carmen Schultze. "Huge swathes of hedges, trees and ivy plants that were growing for decades were irreparably destroyed.

"Many birds and animals in Tiergarten perished," she added. "The ground was so saturated with nitrates and phosperous from huge amounts of urine and faeces that it will take 10 years to recover. The ecosystem won't survive another Love Parade."
A ruling on the injunction, which the local Tiergarten district council also backs, is due on or after June 24.

There are powerful forces, however, who strongly support the Love Parade -- including Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen. In a city starved of a tourist attractions since the Berlin Wall was dismantled in 1989, the parade is a godsend.

"It is delightful to see the images that the Love Parade transmits around the world of young people having great fun with their enthusiasm for music in Berlin in a peaceful fashion," Diepgen told Raveline magazine.
Love Parade press officer Peter Luetzenkirchen said the parade would have to be cancelled this year if the local adminstrative court rules in favour of the environmentalists.
CONFIDENT THAT PARADE WILL PREVAIL

Luetzenkirchen is confident the parade will prevail in court because, he said, it is a demonstration and the German constitution guarantees the right to hold demonstrations when and wherever organisers choose.

"The Love Parade is a demonstration for peace, tolerance, brotherhood, and a fairer distribution of the world's food," Luetzenkirchen said. "The constitution says we can gather wherever we want and no one can stop us."

The BUND says it is a farce to call the event a "demonstration" because of the amount of money paid by tobacco companies and other sponsors to have their names on many of the 40 "floats" -- trucks carrying disc jockeys playing the furious techno music on huge loudspeakers.

"It is absurd to call something a demonstration when they sell exclusive sponsorship and broadcasting rights," Schultze said. "This is a commercial event and a lot of people are going to make a lot of money from it."
It is hard to believe anything called the Love Parade could stir such passions.
NO STRANGER TO CONTROVERSY
But it is not the first time controversy has hit the festival which has grown each year from a modest start in 1989 with 150 people taking part to 750,000 in 1996.
The parade originally ran down the elegant Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard, but stores and local authorities complained bitterly about extensive damage after the 1995 event.

Love Parade organisers wanted to move their party to the historic east Berlin avenue Unter den Linden, but the city baulked at the idea, worried that ravers would damage the lime trees after which it is named.

The parade moved last year from Kurfuerstendamm to its current route along the Strasse der 17 Juni, an eight-lane boulevard, through the heart of the five km (three-mile)- long Tiergarten to the Brandenburg Gate where the Berlin Wall once stood.
Beginning in the early afternoon, the parade culminates just before midnight with all 40 floats gathering at the Prussian Victory Column in the middle of the Tiergarten for a final bash.

Environmental groups first urged the organisers to build fences alongside the road to keep revellers from destroying the plant and animal life. They refused, citing the dangers the fences would cause if there were a panic.

The worries are not entirely unjustified, even though police said last year's parade was mostly peaceful with few incidents. Many revellers fuel their dance marathon with drugs such as ecstasy, cocaine and amphetamines.
"Naturally there will be some damage to the plants and animals in Tiergarten, but human lives are more important than plants," Luetzenkirchen said.
"The whole dispute and all the moaning and groaning is so typical for Berlin.

"The Berliner isn't happy unless he has something to complain about. But for one day at the Love Parade, those grouchy Berliners turn into happy people. It brings out the best in them, their tolerance, their joie de vivre."
The Love Parade pleases Berlin's hoteliers and tourist industry, in a deep slump since the Wall vanished.
Even luxury hotels get into the spirit by tailoring their accommodation for the young crowd. Many cut their rates and stage "Love Parade warm-up parties" for their youthful guests.
Parade veterans say it is not uncommon to see teenagers and octogenerians spontaneously dancing with each other to the 150 beat-per-minute techno sounds at the hotel breakfast buffets.
Many hotels have been sold out for months for the parade, which last year brought 110 million marks ($63.7 million) to Berlin's economy.
But wary of the complaints from the environmental lobby, Diepgen urged the party-goers to watch out for the flowers.

"I would kindly request that you ravers treat the Tiergarten with the respect it deserves," Diepgen said. "Hundreds of thousands of Berliners love the Tiergarten and they are only lending you their park for one day." ($ = 1.728 German Marks)
